walkthroughs.body_html:
Reactions either release energy or take it.

Exothermic reactions give out heat — the surroundings get hotter. Examples: burning fuels, neutralisation, hand warmers.

Endothermic reactions take heat in — the surroundings get colder. Examples: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, sports cold packs.

Breaking bonds always needs energy — it's endothermic.

Making bonds always releases energy — it's exothermic.

If more energy comes out making new bonds than goes in breaking old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall. If the opposite, it's endothermic.

A reaction profile shows energy from reactants to products.

An exothermic profile starts high and ends low — products have less energy than reactants.

An endothermic profile starts low and ends high — products have more energy than reactants.

The hump in the middle is the activation energy — the push needed to get going.

mcqs.q: Burning methane warms the room. This reaction is.
options: Endothermic
Exothermic
Neither — energy is unchanged
Only exothermic at high pressure

mcqs.q: Which statement about bonds is correct?
options: Breaking bonds releases energy
Making bonds takes energy in
Breaking bonds takes energy in; making bonds releases energy
Both breaking and making bonds release energy

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens energetically with the bonds?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Energy released forming new bonds exceeds energy absorbed breaking existing bonds.
Bond breaking releases energy and bond making absorbs energy.
The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
